verdict:
This is a legal procedural novel set in the Lancashire cotton-country of 1926-1927, driven by a single withheld question: can a forged probate document be defeated by the paper trail it contradicts? The book's propulsive engine is not plot-and-jeopardy in the thriller sense but accumulation — a dozen closed doors, each one a chapter, each one an innocent explanation eliminated by a document already in the file. The hearing-date countdown, decreasing in working-note margins chapter by chapter from 290 days to zero, is the visible skeleton of that accumulation. It works, until it idles in the middle, and then it works again at the end.

The first five chapters are excellent. The setup is exact and dry in the way that earns its dryness; Garside's death in Chapter 5 transforms the story at a stroke, placing everything on a solicitor who has been building the record without knowing what it will need to show, alone, with an inheritance and an institution both on the line. The or/and revelation in Chapters 16 and 17 — the forged codicil misquotes the instrument it purports to revoke, substituting "and her issue" for "or her issue" — is a perfect payoff: the clue was present in Chapter 2, it was earned by every chapter before Chapter 17, and it arrives with the simplicity of a lock opening. The corridor scene in Chapter 19, where Walter reads the executed first codicil for the first time and goes still, is the kind of climax that prefers accuracy to drama and loses nothing by the preference.

The middle stalls. Chapters 6 through 12 are structured near-identically: Prescott examines a document, writes a working note, dates it, and leaves the office. There is no adversarial pressure in this book for sixteen chapters; Walter Eccleston, the forger, appears once in Chapter 2, is glimpsed crossing a mill yard in Chapter 9, and is otherwise absent. A forgery driven by a man's desperation can sustain a reader's attention only if the forger's desperation has some presence in the narrative — here it is filed rather than felt. The banking letters in Chapter 11 supply motive as exhibits, but the chapter is the book's lowest-energy passage by some margin: mortgage arithmetic, banking correspondence columns, a financial summary without a scene or a revelation.

The climax's discharge is too brief. Two hundred and ninety days have been counting down; the hearing resolves in a corridor in three minutes. This is structurally correct — the case was already won before the courtroom — but as a reader experience it leaves the accumulated pressure with nowhere sufficient to go. And the Fairhursts, the people this action was for, receive a quarter-page of resolution in the final chapter. Nora's response to winning is noted as "quieter than Prescott had expected," which points at something the book hasn't built. George asks about the mill workers in Chapter 13 and asks again in Chapter 20; the second answer adds nothing the first didn't withhold. An emotional debt is acknowledged rather than paid.

strongest.claim: The or/and revelation is a genuine payoff that plays completely fair: the first codicil is quoted with 'or her issue' in Chapter 1, the forged recital says 'and her issue' from Chapter 2 onward, and the discovery in Chapter 17 rewards any reader attentive enough to have noticed the variance — while not penalising those who weren't. The forger reproduced the date (which the firm's notice letter supplied in writing) but not the operative word (which only the executed document contained), and the mechanism is both elegant and exact.

Garside's death transforms the book without a word of sentiment: the uncapped pen and dried ink are the death, not a scene of grief. The move from two men maintaining a firm to one man carrying a case he did not build — 'Neither of them used those words' about the firm's new name — raises the stakes permanently and gives the subsequent investigative chapters a human cost they would otherwise lack.

Nora Fairhurst functions as the book's human conscience in a narrative dominated by documents and procedures. Her Bank Parade scenes — standing when Prescott enters because she has decided not to sit until she understands what is happening; her observation about Walter that 'he was sorry in the way people are when they have done something they believe they had to do' — give the legal accumulation its stakes and its emotional point of return.

The corridor climax works precisely because it refuses drama. Walter reads the executed first codicil, slows, goes back a line, and goes still — observed, not narrated internally, not explained. The prose stays on the outside of his face. The book has spent eighteen chapters establishing that the law's record is more reliable than any witness, and the climax enacts that thesis: the document in Walter's hands does the work that no confrontation or confession could.

The strong-room register — Garside's habit of recording more than any statute required — is the book's structural spine and its central irony. Introduced in Chapter 1, recognised as decisive in Chapter 5, declared as proof in Chapter 7, and closed with Prescott's own entry in Chapter 20, the register shows that a record built in excess of requirement is the one that survives every attack the forger can mount. The device is sustained without being laboured.

weakest.claim: Chapters 6 through 12 have near-identical architecture: examine a document or source, write a working note, date it, leave the office. The closing gesture — Prescott files the note, picks up his hat, walks out into the square — appears, with minor variation, in every one of these seven chapters. What begins as a rhythm becomes a tic, and the reader's sense that the case is accumulating rather than escalating is accurate: each chapter closes a door, but no chapter opens a danger.

Walter Eccleston, the antagonist, has almost no presence in the narrative for sixteen chapters. He appears for one composed scene in Chapter 2, as a distant back-view in Chapter 9, and as the object of a Thurston and Marsh inquiry letter in Chapter 18. The forgery was driven by desperate financial need — the banking letters in Chapter 11 establish this clearly — but that desperation never generates a scene, a pressure, or a counter-move. Without adversarial friction, the accumulating investigation has nothing to push against.

The hearing, after a 290-day countdown in the margins of twenty chapters, resolves in approximately three minutes of corridor action. The structural logic is sound — the case was already decided before the courtroom — but as a discharge of pressure the climax is proportionally mismatched to the build. A reader who has been counting the days with Prescott may feel the ending goes past before they can turn to meet it.

Chapter heading format is inconsistent across the manuscript: Chapters 1 through 3 use Arabic numerals ('Chapter 1 —', 'Chapter 2 —', 'Chapter 3 —'), Chapters 4 through 6 switch to written-out ordinals ('Chapter Four —', 'Chapter Five —', 'Chapter Six —'), and Chapters 7 through 20 carry only their titles with no ordinal at all. This is a production artifact — the residue of different drafting states in different parts of the manuscript — not a deliberate formal gesture.

George Fairhurst asks what happens to the mill workers in Chapter 13 ('the men lose their jobs') and asks the identical question at the end of Chapter 20 ('what happens to the men'). The second answer — 'the men pass with the sale' — is technically correct but adds nothing the first withholding didn't already establish. A repeated question is a promise of deeper treatment; here the second repetition closes without earning its return.

quotes.text: the pen lay on the page, still uncapped, the ink dried in the nib before anyone had thought to close it.
quotes.why: This is doing what an ordinary 'he was found dead at his desk' line would not: the uncapped pen registers the abruptness of the death through a specific office object, without a single word of emotion. The ink dried in the nib is a duration compressed into a detail — time passed before anyone moved. The sentence is efficient grief.

quotes.text: And the file was going to prove a forgery.
quotes.why: The simplest declarative in the book, and the most important structural pivot. After six chapters of procedural accumulation that has named everything except itself, this sentence is the engine finally speaking plainly. The 'And' at the start earns its place: it is the conclusion of a sequence, not the beginning of one.

quotes.text: The recital said and. The executed instrument said or.
quotes.why: The central revelation stripped to its barest form: two sentences, three words of substance. What makes this excellent rather than merely clever is that it was earned — the 'or' is in the executed codicil in Chapter 1, the 'and' is in the forged recital from Chapter 2, and the gap between them is everything. The book plays completely fair and the revelation rewards exactly the level of attention the prose has trained the reader to give.

quotes.text: He had been wrong since March 1924 and had not known it.
quotes.why: Morally exact. Walter built the forgery on a misheard word — 'and' rather than 'or', a distinction that cannot survive the passage from page to voice. His crime was committed in the name of an entitlement that was itself founded on an error of hearing. The sentence doesn't excuse him; it explains why the forgery is structurally inevitable from the moment it was conceived.

quotes.text: He was not a monster. He went down anyway.
quotes.why: The book's thesis in two declaratives. The first sentence withholds condemnation; the second withholds sympathy. Together they say what a paragraph of analysis would not: the law is not in the business of moral calibration, and the record is not interested in what a man believed he had to do. 'He went down anyway' is also structurally precise — 'anyway' acknowledges the mitigation and dismisses it in one word.

put_down_points: Chapter 11 (The Sale Contract): mortgage arithmetic, banking correspondence, and a financial summary without a human scene or new revelation. The Walter-to-Holt letters supply motive but arrive as exhibits, not drama. This is the book's lowest-energy chapter and the most likely stopping point for a reader who came for the puzzle rather than the procedure.

Chapters 6 through 8 (The Letter-Book, The File, The Gazette): three consecutive chapters with near-identical beats — examine, note, exit — and no adversarial presence to generate friction. A reader who has understood the investigative method from Chapters 1 through 5 may feel these chapters repeat rather than escalate, and the daily days-remaining count in the margins, however elegant in isolation, starts to feel mechanical across three uniform chapters in a row.
who_is_this_for: Readers of historical fiction who prize archival procedure over confrontation — the document-room readers, those who find the Mantel of the Cromwell novels more satisfying than any courtroom drama. Practitioners and former practitioners of law will find specific pleasures in the period accuracy and the silent technical jokes (the Wills Act reference, the solemn-form/common-form distinction, the administrator pendente lite). Readers who need a sympathetic or psychologically developed antagonist, scenes of spoken conflict, or a climax with physical or emotional intensity will be frustrated. The pleasures here are quiet and cumulative: a case built entirely from paper, and the slow revelation that the forgery was betrayed by a single word the forger had never been close enough to read.
